title: Systems thinking and mapping
summary: See a product as a system of people, money and loops, so you can predict what a change will really do.

lessons.title: Products are systems
teach: A product is not just an app. It is a system: users, partners, money, data and rules that all affect each other.
Change one part and others move too. Give riders big discounts on a ride app, and soon there may not be enough drivers.
Systems thinking means asking: 'If I change this, what else changes, and then what?'

questions.prompt: Swiggy cuts restaurant commission sharply. What could happen next?
options: More restaurants join, but Swiggy earns less per order unless it finds money elsewhere
questions.explain: Lower commission attracts restaurants but hurts earnings per order. Thinking one step further shows the trade-off.

questions.prompt: In a system, a fix in one place can create a problem in another place.
questions.explain: Faster delivery targets can push riders to drive unsafely. That's why guardrails exist.

questions.prompt: Put this chain of effects in order for a big rider discount on a ride app.
questions.explain: A change that looks good first can backfire a few steps later.

questions.prompt: Match each part of Zomato's system to its role.

pairs.right: Carry food and earn per trip
Matches all three and sets the rules

questions.explain: Seeing each player helps you predict who wins or loses from a change.

questions.prompt: Which line ignores the system?
lines: If we raise fees, some users may order less
If we add more stores, delivery gets faster
If we cut rider pay, nothing else will change
If we add ads, brands pay us more
questions.explain: Lower rider pay can mean fewer riders, slower delivery and unhappy users.

questions.prompt: What's a 'second order effect'?
options: A result of a result: what happens after the first change
questions.explain: First order: discounts bring users. Second order: those users may only come back for discounts.

questions.prompt: Systems thinking is only useful for very large companies.
questions.explain: Even a small marketplace has buyers, sellers and money moving between them.

lessons.title: Loops: things that feed themselves
teach: A reinforcing loop is a cycle that grows itself: more users bring more content, which brings more users. YouTube works like this.
A balancing loop pulls things back: higher prices reduce demand, which pulls prices down.
Great products find a reinforcing loop and keep feeding it.

questions.prompt: Put YouTube's loop in order.
steps: Creators earn more and want to upload
Better recommendations and more reasons to watch
questions.explain: Each step feeds the next, and the last feeds the first again. That's a reinforcing loop.

questions.prompt: Which is a balancing loop?
options: More friends join, so the app is more useful
Surge pricing raises prices, so fewer people ask for rides
questions.explain: Surge pulls demand down and pulls drivers in, bringing the system back to balance.

questions.prompt: Reinforcing loops can also work in reverse and shrink a product.
questions.explain: If users leave, creators leave, so even more users leave. Many social apps died this way.

questions.prompt: Match each product to its main loop.

pairs.right: More hosts bring more guests, which bring more hosts
More users give more traffic data, which makes maps better
More members make the network more useful to join
More sellers mean more choice and lower prices, bringing more buyers

questions.explain: Each loop explains why the leader is hard to catch.

questions.prompt: Which is not a reinforcing loop?
lines: More players make a game more fun, bringing more players
More data makes the AI better, bringing more users and data
More reviews make buyers trust sellers, bringing more sales and reviews
questions.explain: That one is balancing. It pulls demand back down.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 parts of Instagram's creator loop.
options: Creators gain fans and post more
questions.explain: Posts, views and follows, and more posting. Servers and hiring support the loop but are not part of it.

questions.prompt: As a PM, how do you use a loop?
options: Find the weakest step and make it stronger
questions.explain: If creators don't get enough views, the loop slows. Strengthen that step and the whole loop speeds up.

lessons.title: Mapping a marketplace
teach: A marketplace connects two groups, like buyers and sellers. Mapping it means drawing who gives what to whom.
The hard part is the start: buyers won't come without sellers, and sellers won't come without buyers. This is the 'chicken and egg' problem.
Most marketplaces solve it by starting small (one city, one category) and helping one side first.

questions.prompt: How did Urban Company likely solve chicken and egg early on?
options: Start in a few cities, train and bring on professionals first
Wait for users to bring workers
questions.explain: Getting good, trained workers first makes the first customers happy, so they come back.

questions.prompt: Put the steps to launch a marketplace in order.
steps: Pick one city and one category
Measure how often buyers find a match
questions.explain: Small and dense first. A busy small market beats an empty big one.

questions.prompt: In most marketplaces, getting the supply side first is easier to control.
questions.explain: You can pay or recruit sellers or drivers directly. Buyers usually come when there is good supply.

questions.prompt: Map who gives what on Airbnb.
questions.explain: Mapping flows shows where money and value move, and where trust is needed.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign the marketplace is unhealthy?
lines: Most searches end in a booking
Buyers often see 'no results' in their area
questions.explain: 'No results' means not enough supply. Buyers will leave.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 numbers that show marketplace health.
options: Share of searches with a match
questions.explain: Matches, repeat buyers and happy sellers. Press and offices don't show health.

questions.prompt: What is 'liquidity' in a marketplace?
options: How likely a buyer or seller is to find a match quickly
questions.explain: High liquidity means a rider gets a cab in minutes and a driver gets a ride quickly.

lessons.title: Network effects and moats
teach: A network effect is when a product becomes more useful as more people use it. WhatsApp is useful because your friends are on it.
A moat is anything that makes it hard for rivals to take your users: network effects, data, brand, switching costs or scale.
Not all growth is a moat. Discounts can be copied tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard to beat WhatsApp in India?
options: Everyone you talk to is already on it
questions.explain: A new app is useless if your friends and family aren't on it. That's a strong network effect.

questions.prompt: Match each moat type to a product.

pairs.right: Microsoft Excel at a large company

questions.explain: Each one makes leaving or copying hard in a different way.

questions.prompt: Big discounts are a strong moat.
questions.explain: Anyone with money can copy a discount. Users leave when it ends.

questions.prompt: Which is not a network effect?
lines: More drivers make pickups faster for riders
More users make a review site more useful
A new office makes the team happier
More players make an online game more fun
questions.explain: A happy team is nice, but it doesn't make the product more useful as more people use it.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 things that give Google Maps a moat.
options: Live traffic data from millions of phones
Years of reviews and business info
questions.explain: Data from users, years of content and default placement are hard to copy.

questions.prompt: Quick commerce apps say their moat is dark store locations. Why could that be weak?
options: Rivals can open stores nearby with enough money
questions.explain: Physical stores help, but well funded rivals can copy them. That's why price wars happen.

questions.prompt: Order these from weakest to strongest moat.
questions.explain: Discounts are copied fast, brands take years, and network effects grow stronger with every user.
